summary:
In a country where the land defines our culture and livelihood, every farming decision carries enormous weight. As Information Systems and software development students from Argentina, we built FieldShift; an open-source web decision-support tool that helps farmers plan crop rotations aided by NASA satellite data.
Users draw a field on an interactive map to automatically query NASA POWER climate records, ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0 properties (with Q0.05–Q0.95 uncertainty bounds), and local territorial data. Farmers can calibrate local parameters—such as hardpan depth (tosca), lab organic carbon, and initial soil conditions—and design custom winter-summer crop sequences.
A three-stage engine then evaluates physical crop suitability, simulates a monthly FAO-56 soil water balance with FAO-33 water and thermal yield penalties, and ranks strategies across 15 environmental and economic criteria using SAW-15 and TOPSIS-15. By exposing every formula, data source, and stress scenario like La Niña droughts, FieldShift delivers transparent, data-driven advice to aid local agricultural production
details:
What Field Shift v4.0 does and how it works Choosing a crop rotation requires balancing soil moisture, organic matter, pest cycles, climate extremes, and farm cash flow simultaneously. A rotation that builds soil carbon in a humid year can fail under shallow hardpans (tosca) or drought stress in another season (Pinto et al., 2017; Bowles et al., 2020). As a university student team (Project UNSE), we developed Field Shift v4.0 as a transparent, four-step MVC web application built on a three-stage scientific pipeline:

  1. Plot Definition & Initial Condition (Step 1): Users trace their plot on satellite imagery (Leaflet + Esri World Imagery), while Turf.js computes WGS84 geodesic area and centroid. Users select a 1-to-6-year horizon (12–72 months) and one of 14 starting field states (e.g., soybean residue, wheat stubble, perennial pasture, bare fallow, or disturbed peanut soil), which sets Month-0 moisture, residue cover, and an illustrative 42-cell NDVI spatial grid.
    • Stage 1 (Non-Compensatory Aptitude Filter): Checks crop water and rooting-depth limits against SoilGrids Q0.05–Q0.95 quantiles and user hardpan depth, flagging each strategy as Suitable, Uncertain (measure on-farm), or Unsuitable.
    • Stage 2 (Monthly FAO-56 Water Balance): Computes reference evapotranspiration (ET0ET_0ET0​) via FAO-56 Penman-Monteith (Allen et al., 1998) and integrates soil water storage monthly in three sub-steps (St=St−1+Pef−ETa−DS_t = S_{t-1} + P_{\text{ef}} - ET_a - DSt​=St−1​+Pef​−ETa​−D, depletion fraction p=0.50p = 0.50p=0.50), tracking water-stress factor KsK_sKs​, deep drainage, soil organic carbon (ΔSOC\Delta SOCΔSOC), and cash flow.
    • Stage 3 (FAO-33 Yield, Thermal Extremes & MCDA): Applies FAO-33 yield sensitivity KyK_yKy​ (Doorenbos & Kassam, 1979), deducts flowering heat (>35°C) and frost (<0°C) days from empirical NASA POWER exceedance curves, auto-calibrates potential yield (YpotY_{\text{pot}}Ypot​) to 10-year district averages, and dynamically scores water balance (C1C_1C1​), thermal resilience (C7C_7C7​), and water use efficiency (C9C_9C9​). Finally, it compares SAW-8, SAW-15, and non-compensatory TOPSIS-15 (Hwang & Yoon, 1981) with 90% confidence bands and stress presets (La Niña drought -30% rain / +2°C, El Niño +30% rain, and price/input shocks).

Benefits, creativity, and intended impact Most farm tools either display raw satellite maps without agronomic interpretation or hide recommendations behind black-box AI. Field Shift is creative in pairing white-box pedagogy (clickable equations, plain-language explanations, and step-by-step animated pointer tutorials) with epistemological honesty: we explicitly separate live satellite/soil observations from district statistics and parameterized crop/spatial layers (such as the 42-cell NDVI grid and SMAP L4 62% baseline fill) (Entekhabi et al., 2010; Reichle et al., 2019). Combining SAW-15 with TOPSIS-15 prevents short-term grain income from masking severe bare-soil erosion or organic carbon depletion (Álvarez et al., 2017; Caviglia et al., 2004; Beillouin et al., 2021; Abdalla et al., 2019). Our intended impact is giving agricultural students, smallholders, and local extensionists an accessible planning sandbox to test long-term resilience before committing seed and fertilizer—while reminding users that final prescriptions require a certified local agronomist.

Tools, languages, and factors considered

  • Backend: Node.js, Express, EJS templates, in-memory TTL caching, and offline JSON fallback (data/zona_guamini_10ha.json).
  • Frontend & Static Explorer: HTML5, CSS3 (light/dark editorial UI, ES/EN toggle), vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet.js (Esri World Imagery), Turf.js (WGS84 geometry), and Chart.js.
  • Key design factors: Rural low-connectivity resilience, explicit soil uncertainty propagation (Q0.05–Q0.95), contractor/livestock machinery constraints (C14), land-tenure cash-flow priorities (C8, C15), and full Apache 2.0 open-source reproducibility.
